label: Definition: Chains of primes, length, and dimension of a ring

source_data: A discrete valuation on a field K is a surjection v:K*→Z satisfying v(xy)=v(x)+v(y) and v(x+y)≥min(v(x),v(y)).

source_data: An A-submodule M⊆K is invertible if MN=A for some N⊆K. The inverse is unique and equals (A:M); every invertible ideal is finitely generated and hence fractional.

label: Definition / comparison: Topological abelian group and zero-neighborhood control
source_data: A topological abelian group has continuous addition and inversion. If {0} is closed then the group is Hausdorff; translations are homeomorphisms, so the topology is determined by the neighborhoods of 0.

label: Definition / construction: Cauchy sequences and completion of a topological abelian group

source_data: Let M be a topological n-manifold. Given a cover U of M; another cover V is called a refinement of U if for each V ∈ mathcal V there exists some U ∈ U such that V ⊆ U . label: Definition/convention — diffeomorphism
source_data: The definition will be based on the calculus of maps between Euclidean spaces, so let us begin by reviewing some basic terminology about such maps. If U and V are open subsets of Euclidean spaces ℝ ^n and ℝ ^m , respectively, a function F : U → V is said to be smooth (or C ^∞ , or infinitely differentiable) if each of its component functions has continuous partial derivatives of all orders. If in addition F is bijective and has a smooth inverse map, it is called a diffeomorphism. A diffeomorphism is, in particular, a homeomorphism. A review of some important properties of smooth maps is given in Appendix C. You should be aware that some authors define the word smooth differently—for example, to mean continuously differentiable or merely differentiable. On the other hand, some use the word differentiable to mean what we call smooth. Throughout this book, smooth is synonymous with C ^∞

label: Definition/convention — transition map
source_data: Let M be a topological n-manifold. If ( U , φ ) , ( V , ψ ) are two charts such that U ∩ V ≠ emptyset , the composite map ∘ φ ^- 1 : φ ( U ∩ V ) → ψ ( U ∩ V ) is called the transition map from ' to (Fig. 1.6). It is a composition of homeomorphisms, and is therefore itself a homeomorphism. Two charts ( U , φ ) and ( V , ψ ) are said to be smoothly compatible if either U ∩ V = emptyset or the transition map ψ ∘ φ ^- 1 is a diffeomorphism. Since φ ( U ∩ V ) and ψ ( U ∩ V ) are open subsets of ℝ ^n , smoothness of this map is to be interpreted in the ordinary sense of having continuous partial derivatives of all orders.

label: Definition/convention — smooth atlas
source_data: We define an atlas for M to be a collection of charts whose domains cover M . An atlas A is called a smooth atlas if any two charts in A are smoothly compatible with each other.

label: Definition/convention — differentiable structures
source_data: Now we can define the main concept of this chapter. If M is a topological manifold, a smooth structure on M is a maximal smooth atlas. A smooth manifold is a pair ( M , A ) , where M is a topological manifold and A is a smooth structure on M . When the smooth structure is understood, we usually omit mention of it and just say ^6 6 M is a smooth manifold.” Smooth structures are also called differentiable structures or C ^∞ structures by some authors. We also use the term smooth manifold structure to mean a manifold topology together with a smooth structure.

label: Comparison/convention — a C
source_data: It is worth mentioning that the notion of smooth structure can be generalized in several different ways by changing the compatibility requirement for charts. For example, if we replace the requirement that charts be smoothly compatible by the weaker requirement that each transition map ∘ φ ^- 1 (and its inverse) be of class C ^k , we obtain the definition of a C ^k structure. Similarly, if we require that each transition map be real-analytic (i.e., expressible as a convergent power series in a neighborhood of each point), we obtain the definition of a real-analytic structure, also called a C ^ω structure. If M has even dimension n = 2 m , we can identify ℝ ^2 m with ℂ ^m and require that the transition maps be complex-analytic; this determines a complex-analytic structure. A manifold endowed with one of these structures is called a C ^k manifold, real-analytic manifold, or complex manifold, respectively. (Note that a C ^0 manifold is just a topological manifold.) We do not treat any of these other kinds of manifolds in this book, but they play important roles in analysis, so it is useful to know the definitions.

source_data: So far in this chapter, all of our submanifolds have been manifolds without boundary. source_data: To begin, we need to make sense of “formal linear combinations.” Let S be a set. Roughly speaking, a formal linear combination of elements of S is an expression of the form scriptstyle sum _i = 1 ^m a _i x _i , where a _1 , … , a _m are real numbers and x _1 , … , x _m are elements of S. Of course, since we are not assuming that S has any algebraic structure, we cannot literally add elements of S together or multiply them by numbers. But the essential feature of such an expression is that it is completely determined by which elements of S appear in the sum, and what coefficients appear with them. Thus, we make the following definition: for any set S, a formal linear combination of elements of S is a function f : S → ℝ such that f ( s ) = 0 for all but finitely many s ∈ S . The free (real) vector space on S , denoted by F ( S ) , is the set of all formal linear combinations of elements of S. Under pointwise addition and scalar multiplication, F ( S ) becomes a vector space over R.

source_data: An important generalization of Riemannian metrics is obtained by relaxing the positivity requirement. A symmetric 2-tensor g on a vector space V is said to be nondegenerate if the linear map hat(g) : V → V * defined by widehat g ( v ) ( w ) = g ( v , w ) is an isomorphism, or equivalently if for every nonzero v ∈ V there exists w ∈ V such that g ( v , w ) ≠ 0 . label: Definition/convention — orientable
source_data: As we will see in this chapter, a vector space always has exactly two choices of orientation. In R n , there is a standard orientation that we can all agree on; but in other vector spaces, an arbitrary choice has to be made. For manifolds, the situation is much more complicated. On a sphere, it is possible to decide unambiguously which rotational direction is counterclockwise, by looking at the surface from the outside (Fig. 15.1). On the other hand, a Möbius band (Fig. 15.2) has the curious property that a figure moving around on the surface can come back to its starting point transformed into its mirror image, so it is impossible to decide consistently which of the two possible rotational directions on the surface to call “clockwise” and which “counterclockwise,” or which is the “front” side and which is the “back” side. The analogous phenomenon in a 3-manifold would be a right-handed person who takes a long trip and comes back left-handed. Manifolds like the sphere, in which it is possible to choose a consistent orientation, are said to be orientable; those like the Möbius band in which it is not possible are said to be nonorientable.

Because d ∘ d = 0 . every exact form is closed. In this chapter, we explore the implications of the converse question: Is every closed form exact? source_data: Suppose we are given an action of a group G on a topological space M; which we write either as θ : G × M → M or as ( g , p ) ↦ g · p . (For definiteness, let us assume that G acts on the left; similar considerations apply to right actions.) Recall that the orbit of a point p ∈ M is the set of images of p under all elements of the group: G · p = g · p: g ∈ G . Define a relation on M by setting p ∼ q if there exists g ∈ G such that g · p = q This is an equivalence relation, whose equivalence classes are exactly the orbits of G in M . The set of orbits is denoted by M / G ; with the quotient topology it is called the orbit space of the action. It is of great importance to determine conditions under which an orbit space is a smooth manifold. It is important to be aware that some authors use the notation G backslash M for an orbit space determined by a left action of G on M; reserving M / G for one determined by a right action. We use only the latter notation, relying on the context, not the notation, to distinguish between the two cases.

source_data: The definition of the Picard group of a one-dimensional noetherian integral domain $\mathcal{O}$ avoids the problem of the uniqueness of prime ideal decomposition by restricting attention to the invertible ideals, and thus leaving aside the information carried by noninvertibles. But there is another important generalization of the ideal class group which does take into account all prime ideals of $\mathcal{O}$ . It is based on an artificial re-introduction of the uniqueness of prime decomposition. This group is called the divisor class group, or Chow group of $\mathcal{O}$ . Its definition starts from the free abelian group $$ D i v (\mathcal {O}) = \bigoplus_ {\mathfrak {p}} \mathbb {Z} \mathfrak {p} $$ on the set of all maximal ideals $\mathfrak{p}$ of $\mathcal{O}$ (i.e., the set of all prime ideals $\neq 0$ ). This group is called the divisor group of $\mathcal{O}$ . Its elements are formal sums $$ D = \sum_ {\mathfrak {p}} n _ {\mathfrak {p}} \mathfrak {p} $$ with $n_{p} \in Z$ and $n_{p} = 0$ for almost all p, called divisors (or 0-cycles). Corollary (3.9) simply says that, in the case of a Dedekind domain, the divisor group $Div(\mathcal{O})$ and the group of ideals are canonically isomorphic. The additive notation and the name of the group stem from function theory where divisors for analytic functions play the same rôle as ideals do for algebraic numbers (see chap. III, §3).

This property may be formulated in a purely algebraic way as follows. Let $a \in C$ be a point in the complex plane. The set of all functions $f(x)$ in the polynomial ring C[x] which vanish at the point a forms the maximal ideal $\mathfrak{p} = (x - a)$ of C[x]. In this way the points of the complex plane correspond 1-1 to the maximal ideals of C[x]. We denote the set of all these maximal ideals by $$ M = \operatorname{Max} (\mathbb {C} [ x ]). $$ We may view M as a new kind of space and may interpret the elements $f(x)$ of the ring C[x] as functions on M as follows. For every point $\mathfrak{p} = (x - a)$ of M we have the canonical isomorphism $$ \mathbb {C} [ x ] / \mathfrak {p} \stackrel {\sim} {\longrightarrow} \mathbb {C}, $$ which sends the residue class $f(x) \mod \mathfrak{p}$ to $f(a)$ . We may thus view this residue class $$ f (\mathfrak {p}) := f (x) \bmod \mathfrak {p} \in \kappa (\mathfrak {p}) $$ in the residue class field $\kappa(\mathfrak{p}) = \mathbb{C}[x]/\mathfrak{p}$ as the “value” of f at the point $p \in M$ . The topology on C cannot be transferred to M by algebraic means. All that can be salvaged algebraically are the point sets defined by equations of the form $$ f (x) = 0 $$ (i.e., only the finite sets and $M$ itself). These sets are defined to be the closed subsets. In the new formulation they are the sets $$ V (f) = \left\{\mathfrak {p} \in M \mid f (\mathfrak {p}) = 0 \right\} = \left\{\mathfrak {p} \in M \mid \mathfrak {p} \supseteq (f (x)) \right\}. $$

source_data: There, on an algebraic $\mathbb{Z}$ -scheme $X$ , one studies on the one hand the totality of all vector bundles, and on the other, that of all irreducible subschemes of $X$ . From the first, one constructs a series of groups $K_{i}(X)$ which constitute the subject of algebraic $K$ -theory. From the second is constructed a series of groups $CH^{i}(X)$ , the subject of Chow theory. Vector bundles are by definition locally free $\mathcal{O}_X$ -modules. In the special case $X = \operatorname{Spec}(\mathcal{O})$ this includes the fractional ideals. The irreducible subschemes and their formal linear combinations, i.e., the cycles of $X$ , are to be considered as generalizations of the primes and divisors. The isomorphism between divisor class group and ideal class group extends to the general setting as a homomorphic relation between the groups $CH^{i}(X)$ and $K_{i}(X)$ . Thus the initial controversy has been resolved into a seminal mathematical theory (for further reading, see [13]).

source_data: Another very interesting functorial property of the reciprocity map is obtained via the transfer (Verlagerung in German). For an arbitrary group G, let $G'$ denote the commutator subgroup and write $$ G ^ {a b} = G / G ^ {\prime} $$ for the maximal abelian quotient group. If then $H \subseteq G$ is a subgroup of finite index, we have a canonical homomorphism $$ \operatorname{Ver}: G ^ {a b} \longrightarrow H ^ {a b}, $$ which is called transfer from G to H. This homomorphism is defined as follows (see [75], chap. IV, §1). Let $R$ be a system of representatives for the left cosets of $H$ in $G$ , $G = RH$ , $1 \in R$ . If $\sigma \in G$ we write, for every $\rho \in R$ , $$ \sigma \rho = \rho^ {\prime} \sigma_ {\rho}, \quad \sigma_ {\rho} \in H, \quad \rho^ {\prime} \in R, $$ and we define $$ \operatorname{Ver} \left(\sigma \bmod G ^ {\prime}\right) = \prod_ {\rho \in R} \sigma_ {\rho} \bmod H ^ {\prime}. $$

This is the question whether the class field tower $$ K = K _ {0} \subseteq K _ {1} \subseteq K _ {2} \subseteq K _ {3} \subseteq \dots , $$ where $K_{i+1}$ is the Hilbert class field of $K_{i}$ , stops after a finite number of steps. A positive answer would have the implication that the last field in the tower had class number 1 so that in it not only the ideals of K, but in fact all its ideals become principal. This perspective naturally generated the greatest interest. But the problem, after withstanding for a long time all attempts to solve it, was finally decided in the negative by the Russian mathematicians E.S. GOLOD and I.R. ŠAFAREVIČ in 1964 (see [48], [24]).

source_data: The zeroes of the Riemann zeta function command special attention. Euler's identity (1.1) shows that one has $\zeta(s) \neq 0$ for $\operatorname{Re}(s) > 1$ . The gamma function $\Gamma(s)$ is nowhere 0 and has simple poles at $s = 0, -1, -2, \ldots$ . The functional equation $Z(s) = Z(1 - s)$ , i.e., $$ \pi^ {- s / 2} \Gamma (s / 2) \zeta (s) = \pi^ {(s - 1) / 2} \Gamma ((1 - s) / 2) \zeta (1 - s), $$ therefore shows that the only zeroes of $\zeta(s)$ in the domain $\operatorname{Re}(s) < 0$ are the poles of $\Gamma(s/2)$ , i.e., the arguments $s = -2, -4, -6, \ldots$ . These are called the trivial zeroes of $\zeta(s)$ . Other zeroes have to lie in the critical strip $0 \leq \operatorname{Re}(s) \leq 1$ , since $\zeta(s) \neq 0$ for $\operatorname{Re}(s) > 1$ . They are the subject of the famous, still unproven Riemann Hypothesis: The non-trivial zeroes of $\zeta(s)$ lie on the line $\operatorname{Re}(s) = \frac{1}{2}$ .

source_data: The degree of a representation $(\rho, V)$ of a finite group G is the dimension of V. The representation is called irreducible if the G-module V does not admit any proper G-invariant subspace. Every representation $(\rho, V)$ factors into a direct sum $$ V = V _ {1} \oplus \dots \oplus V _ {s} $$ of irreducible representations. If an irreducible representation $(\rho_{\alpha}, V_{\alpha})$ is equivalent to precisely $r_{\alpha}$ among the representations in this decomposition, then $r_{\alpha}$ is called the multiplicity of $\rho_{\alpha}$ in $\rho$ , and one writes $$ \rho \sim \sum_ {\alpha} r _ {\alpha} \rho_ {\alpha}, $$ where $\rho_{\alpha}$ varies over all non-equivalent irreducible representations of G.

The zero section of the disc bundle is a string of complex projective lines $E ^ { ( n + 1 ) } : = E _ { 1 } \cup \cdot \cdot \cdot \cup E _ { n + 1 }$ whose intersection behaviour is given by the graph $\Gamma _ { ( - m _ { 0 } , . . . , - m _ { n } ) }$ where $- t / s = [ - m _ { n } , \ldots , - m _ { 0 } ]$ . Hence $E _ { j } \cdot E _ { j } = - m _ { j }$ , and consecutively numbered $E _ { j }$ meet transversely in a point and there are no other intersections between the curves $E _ { j }$ . The graph $\Gamma _ { ( - m _ { 0 } , . . . , - m _ { n } ) }$ is called the dual graph of the configuration consisting of the $E _ { j }$ . Glueing $Y ( t , s )$ and $\mathbb { C } ^ { 2 } - \{ 0 \}$ along $Y ( t , s ) - E ^ { ( n + 1 ) }$ results in a complex surface $\widetilde { W _ { t , s } }$ together with a holomorphic map $\pi : \widetilde { W _ { t , s } } \longrightarrow W _ { t , s }$ which is biholomorphic outside $E ^ { ( n + 1 ) }$ and contracts $E ^ { ( n + 1 ) }$ to the singularity at $0$ . The subvariety $E ^ { ( n + 1 ) }$ is called the exceptional divisor. A holomorphic map such as $\pi$ from a smooth surface to a surface with an isolated singularity $p$ and which is biholomorphic outside $\pi ^ { - 1 } p$ is a resolution of the singularity $p$ . The simplest example is the singularity $A _ { 2 , 1 }$ , an ordinary double point with local equation $u v = w ^ { 2 }$ . The exceptional subvariety consists of a single $\mathbb { P } ^ { 1 }$ with self-intersection $- 2$ . More generally, we may consider $A _ { n + 1 , n }$ with local equation $u v = w ^ { n + 1 }$ . (4.8) one has $\textstyle { \frac { n + 1 } { n } } = [ 2 , 2 , \dotsc , 2 ]$ ( $n$ times), and so the exceptional set consists of a string of $n$ curves with self-intersection $- 2$ . source_data: Reed-Muller codes. The definition of this class of codes runs as follows. Let $I$ be a finite set of size $N$ . Then the functions $I \to \mathbb { F } _ { 2 }$ form the $\mathbb { F } _ { 2 }$ -vector space $\mathbb { F } _ { 2 } ^ { I }$ Suppose that itself consists of the points of an $\mathbb { F } _ { 2 }$ -vector space $W$ of dimension $m$ so that $N = 2 ^ { m }$ . We order these points as follows. Let $\{ e _ { 0 } , \dotsc , e _ { m - 1 } \}$ be a basis for $W$ and identify a point $\begin{array} { r } { x = \sum _ { j = 0 } ^ { m - 1 } x _ { j } e _ { j } } \end{array}$ with the binary expansion $\begin{array} { r } { n _ { x } = \sum _ { j = 0 } ^ { m - 1 } x _ { j } 2 ^ { j } } \end{array}$ of an integer between 0 and $2 ^ { m } - 1$ . The natural order gives an ordering of the points of $W$ . An ?? $^ 2$ -valued function $f$ on $W$ determines a vector $( f _ { 0 } , \dotsc , f _ { N - 1 } ) \in \mathbb { F } _ { 2 } ^ { N }$ as follows. First note that a point $x \in W$ determines the unique integer $j = n _ { x } \ \in$ $\lfloor 0 , \ldots , N - 1 \rfloor$ and then we set $f _ { j } = f ( x )$ . This way, the polynomial functions of degree $k$ on $W$ together with the zero function define a subspace of $\mathbb { F } _ { 2 } ^ { N }$ and this is also the case for polynomial functions of degree $\leq k$ . For $0 \leq k < m$ , the latter define the $k$ -th order Reed–Muller code $S ^ { \le k } ( W ) \subset \mathbb { F } _ { 2 } ^ { N }$ , $N = 2 ^ { m }$ . For an extensive treatment of these codes we refer to [140, Sect. 4.5.].

source_data: 5.2.A Even sets of nodes. Let $Y$ be a (connected compact and smooth) complex surface which is the minimal resolution of a singular surface $Y ^ { \prime }$ having a finite set of ordinary double points (and no other singularities). The example to have in mind is the (singular) Kummer surface (see Appendix B.3). As in that example, each double point is resolved by a nodal curve, by definition a smooth rational curve with self-intersection $- 2$ . Conversely, such a curve can be contracted to give a surface with an ordinary double point. A special role is played by subsets $\{ E _ { j } \} _ { j \in J }$ of disjoint nodal curves for which $\begin{array} { r } { B _ { J } = \sum _ { j \in J } E _ { j } \in 2 \mathsf { N S } ( Y ) } \end{array}$ . Such a set is called an even set of nodal curves.3 Its role is highlighted by the following geometric construction. source_data: The spin group of a quadratic vector space $( V , q )$ over a field $k$ is defined by means of its Clifford algebra ${ \mathsf { C } } ( q )$ . As a vector space this is just the exterior algebra $\Lambda ( V )$ and it contains $V$ . The algebra structure comes from $q$ . For us its importance lies in the action of the algebra conjugation. Firstly, conjugation with a non-isotropic vector $u \in V$ preserves $V$ and, secondly, in $V$ this gives the hyperplane reflection $\sigma _ { u }$ up to a sign. This property for $u$ can be extended to a ”large” subgroup of ${ \mathsf { C } } ( q )$ . To do this properly, one makes use of a canonical splitting of ${ \mathsf { C } } ( q )$ into even and odd elements. The even elements form a subalgebra, the even Clifford algebra. The conjugation with $u$ receives a sign according to whether $u$ is odd or even. The Clifford group consists of the invertible elements $u$ of the Clifford algebra which have the property that twisted conjugation with $u$ preserves $V$ .

label: Definition: separable k-algebra

label: Definition: linear disjointness

source_data: A chain complex K has d²=0 and homology H_n=ker d_n/im d_{n+1}; a cochain complex has cohomology H^n=ker d^n/im d^{n−1}. Exactness means all homology vanishes.

label: Definition: morphism of complexes

kind: Definition: chain homotopy and homotopy equivalence
label: Definition: chain homotopy and homotopy equivalence
source_data: Morphisms f,g are homotopic if f−g=dh+hd. Homotopic maps induce the same homology map; homotopy-equivalent complexes have isomorphic homology.

label: Theorem/construction: long exact homology sequence

kind: Definition: double complex and total complex

label: Definition: projective module
source_data: P is projective if maps P→N lift across every surjection M→N. Projective modules are exactly direct summands of free modules.

label: Definition: injective module
source_data: I is injective if maps from submodules extend across injections, the arrow-dual lifting condition to projectivity.

label: Definition/construction: projective resolution
source_data: Every module M has a projective resolution ⋯→P_1→P_0→M→0 built by successive projective surjections; its positive homology vanishes and H_0≅M.

label: Definition/construction: injective resolution
source_data: Every module M embeds into an injective resolution 0→M→Q^0→Q^1→⋯ with H^0≅M and H^n=0 for n>0.

label: Definition: Tor functors

label: Definition: Ext functors

label: Definition: projective and injective dimension
source_data: projdim M is the least length of a projective resolution, or ∞; injdim is defined dually. Dimension zero is equivalent to projectivity/injectivity.

label: Definition/theorem: derived functors

search_key: canonical Levi factor of a standard parabolic

label: iterated unipotent-normalizer sequence P(U)
source_data: For closed unipotent U, repeatedly enlarge U_i by R_u(N_G(U_i)) and take the next normalizer until stabilization; the terminal normalizer is denoted P(U).

label: weights and multiplicities of a rational representation
source_data: For a rational G-module V, a weight is a character λ∈X(T) with V_λ={v \
search_key: weights and multiplicities of a rational representation

label: abstract weight lattice and dominant weights
source_data: Every representation weight is an abstract weight: its Cartan integers against all roots are integral. Abstract weights form a lattice Λ containing the root lattice Λ_r with finite index; a base gives fundamental dominant weights and the dominant cone.
search_key: abstract weight lattice and dominant weights

label: fundamental group, simply connected type and adjoint type
source_data: For semisimple G, π(G)=Λ/X(T). G is simply connected (universal type) when X(T)=Λ, and of adjoint type when X(T)=Λ_r.
search_key: fundamental group, simply connected type and adjoint type

label: maximal vector
source_data: A nonzero v in a rational G-module is maximal relative to B when Kv is B-stable, equivalently v is a weight vector fixed by all positive root groups.

label: irreducible rational G-module
source_data: A nonzero rational G-module is irreducible when its only G-stable subspaces are 0 and itself.

label: addition of highest weights under tensor products
source_data: If V,V′ contain maximal vectors of weights λ,μ, then their tensor product contains a maximal vector of weight λ+μ; hence existence for λ and μ implies existence for λ+μ.
search_key: addition of highest weights under tensor products

label: maximal-parabolic representations realizing multiples of fundamental weights
source_data: Chevalley’s stabilizer theorem applied to maximal parabolics P_{Δ−{α_i}} gives rational modules with maximal vectors of weights d_iω_i for positive integers d_i.
search_key: maximal-parabolic representations realizing multiples of fundamental weights

label: canonical highest-weight matrix coefficient
source_data: Given highest vector v_λ and dual functional r selecting it, c_λ(g)=r(gv_λ) is a regular matrix coefficient satisfying c_λ(xgy)=λ(x) c_λ(g) λ(y) for x in the opposite Borel and y in B, with the corresponding conventions.

label: function-space realization of highest-weight modules
source_data: For dominant λ, the semi-invariant function space F_λ⊆K[G] defined by left opposite-Borel covariance is right-translation stable; its canonical maximal vector c_λ generates the irreducible module V(λ), and in characteristic zero F_λ itself is irreducible by complete reducibility.

label: minimal dominant highest weights
source_data: A dominant λ is minimal when no smaller dominant weight exists. Then V(λ) has exactly the W-orbit of λ as its weights, each with multiplicity one, so dim V(λ)=\

label: rank-one and rank-two reductive subgroups used in classification
source_data: For simple roots α,β, set Z_α=C_G(T_α) and Z_{αβ}=C_G((T_α∩T_β)°). The latter is reductive of semisimple rank two with root subsystem generated by α,β and is a Levi factor of the corresponding standard parabolic.
search_key: rank-one and rank-two reductive subgroups used in classification

label: isogeny of algebraic groups
source_data: An isogeny G→G′ is a surjective morphism of algebraic groups with finite kernel.

label: rank-two compatibility conditions (A), (B), (C)
source_data: The extension proof is reduced to three rank-two conditions: compatibility of Coxeter relations in N; compatibility of root-group isomorphisms on U_{αβ}; and compatibility of conjugation by chosen simple-reflection representatives.

label: coroot system in the cocharacter lattice
source_data: For each simple α, the rank-one subgroup determines a cocharacter α∨ with ⟨α,α∨⟩=2 and t_α=α∨(−1). These coroots form the dual root system Φ∨ in R⊗Y(T), with Weyl action governed by the Cartan integers.
search_key: coroot system in the cocharacter lattice

label: Chevalley construction and existence of all semisimple types
source_data: Chevalley’s integral-basis construction produces adjoint groups over arbitrary fields; projective-representation or integral highest-weight methods then produce simply connected and intermediate forms, yielding semisimple groups with every allowed fundamental group.
search_key: Chevalley construction and existence of all semisimple types

label: k-closed subset and Zariski k-topology
source_data: For k⊆K, a closed subset of affine space is k-closed when it is the zero set of polynomials with coefficients in k; these sets define the Zariski k-topology.
mapping_hint: k-closed sets and the k-Zariski topology assemble from polynomial zero loci

label: variety defined over k
source_data: An affine variety is defined over k when its radical vanishing ideal is generated by its intersection with k[T]; intrinsically this gives a k-form k[X] with K[X]≅K⊗_k k[X], and the notion extends by affine coverings.
mapping_hint: affine descent definition and intrinsic base-change form assemble from native ideals, quotients and schemes over a base

label: k-rational points
source_data: For a variety X defined over k, X(k) is its intrinsically defined set of k-rational points; in affine coordinates it is X∩k^n.
mapping_hint: k-rational points are native sections over Spec k

label: morphism defined over k
source_data: A morphism between varieties defined over k is a k-morphism when its affine coordinate maps are defined over k; this is intrinsic and local on affine coverings.
mapping_hint: k-morphisms are native morphisms in the over-category

label: algebraic group defined over k
source_data: A k-group is an algebraic group whose group variety, multiplication and inversion are defined over k. G(k) is then an abstract subgroup; the standard linear groups are defined over their prime field.
mapping_hint: k-group definition and rational-point group are native; blanket prime-field statement for all standard linear groups remains only partially checked

label: k-morphic action and rationality of transporters
source_data: An action is k-morphic when group, variety and action map are defined over k. For k-rational source subsets and k-closed target sets, transporters, corresponding centralizers and fixed sets are k-closed.
search_key: k-morphic action and rationality of transporters
mapping_hint: k-morphic-action definition is native; k-closedness of transporters and fixed loci remains a theorem gap

label: k-torus, k-split and k-anisotropic torus
source_data: A torus defined over k is k-split when its k-defined characters span its coordinate algebra, equivalently it is k-isomorphic to G_m^d; it is k-anisotropic when it has no nontrivial k-defined character.
mapping_hint: k-torus, split and anisotropic predicates are reference-owned character-lattice data

label: k-split and k-anisotropic reductive group
source_data: A reductive k-group is k-split when it has a k-split maximal torus and compatible root-subgroup parametrizations over k; it is k-anisotropic when it has no positive-dimensional k-split torus.
mapping_hint: anisotropic predicate is direct; k-split reductive structure still lacks the required relative root-subgroup package

label: k-rank, k-roots and k-Weyl group
source_data: Choose a maximal k-split torus S. Its dimension is rank_k G. The nonzero weights of Ad S are the k-roots; with Z=C_G(S), N=N_G(S), the finite quotient W_k=N/Z is the k-Weyl group.
mapping_hint: conditional rank/weight/normalizer definitions are native; finiteness and relative-root identification remain unchecked

label: nonreduced root system and type BC
source_data: Dropping the axiom excluding 2α alongside α gives nonreduced root systems. The only irreducible nonreduced family is BC_r, with no new Weyl groups beyond types B_r/C_r.
search_key: nonreduced root system and type BC
mapping_hint: nonreduced root-pairing notion is native; BC classification is absent

label: elementary subgroup generated by minimal-parabolic unipotent radicals
source_data: For non-anisotropic G, G* is generated by U(k) over unipotent radicals of minimal k-parabolics. The source records Tits’s simplicity result for G*/Z(G*) in the simple case for most k, and notes that G(k)=G* often but not always holds for simply connected semisimple groups.
search_key: elementary subgroup generated by minimal-parabolic unipotent radicals
mapping_hint: elementary subgroup definition is generic once radicals exist; Tits simplicity/equality theorems remain absent

label: k-quasisplit group
source_data: A semisimple k-group is k-quasisplit when it has a Borel subgroup defined over k.
mapping_hint: k-quasisplit is the native Borel-over-the-base predicate

label: nonarchimedean local field
source_data: The source uses “local field” for a completion with respect to a discrete nonarchimedean valuation, with valuation ring R, maximal ideal P=(π), and residue field R/P.
mapping_hint: nonarchimedean local field and its valuation-ring data are native

label: anisotropic kernel
source_data: For maximal k-split S with Z=C_G(S), the anisotropic kernel is the product of (Z,Z) with the maximal anisotropic k-torus in Z(Z); it is a maximal reductive k-anisotropic subgroup, determined up to k-isomorphism.
mapping_hint: anisotropic-kernel ingredients are available, but maximality/uniqueness is not

label: Tits index
source_data: The Tits index records the absolute Dynkin diagram, the subset of simple roots vanishing on S (the anisotropic kernel nodes), and the Galois action on the remaining diagram; roots in a common orbit have the same restriction to S.
mapping_hint: Tits-index data are direct; compatibility of Galois orbits with restricted roots remains unchecked

label: reflection relative to a root vector
source_data: A reflection relative to nonzero α sends α to −α and fixes a hyperplane pointwise. If a finite spanning set Φ is reflection-stable, the reflection attached to α∈Φ is uniquely determined.
search_key: reflection relative to a root vector
mapping_hint: reflections relative to a root vector and uniqueness are library-owned

label: abstract root system
source_data: An abstract root system Φ⊂E is finite, spans E, omits 0, has only ±α on each root line, is stable under a reflection s_α for each root, and satisfies the integral Cartan condition s_α(β)−β∈Zα. Root-system isomorphisms preserve these integers; rank is dim E.

label: Weyl group and invariant inner product
source_data: W(Φ)=⟨s_α⟩ is finite and preserves an inner product for which s_α(β)=β−⟨β,α⟩α with Cartan integer ⟨β,α⟩=2(β,α)/(α,α).
search_key: Weyl group and invariant inner product
mapping_hint: Weyl group, invariant form and reflection formula are native; explicit finiteness theorem remains unlocated

label: bases, Weyl chambers and positive roots
source_data: A base Δ is a vector-space basis in which each root has integral coefficients all of one sign. Bases exist, W acts simply transitively on them, and they correspond to Weyl chambers; they define simple, positive and negative roots and the recorded two-root reduction properties.
search_key: bases, Weyl chambers and positive roots
mapping_hint: bases, base existence and positive roots are native; chamber correspondence and simple transitivity remain absent

label: length in a Weyl group
source_data: W is generated by simple reflections. The length of w is its minimal simple-reflection word length and equals the number of positive roots sent negative; a simple reflection permutes all positive roots except its own root.
mapping_hint: simple-reflection generation is native; Coxeter length/inversion-count theorem is absent

label: irreducible root systems and their decomposition
source_data: Φ is irreducible when it cannot be split into mutually orthogonal proper root subsets. Every root system decomposes uniquely into irreducible components.
search_key: irreducible root systems and their decomposition
mapping_hint: irreducibility predicate is native; unique orthogonal decomposition remains absent

label: abstract weight lattice and fundamental group table
source_data: Abstract weights λ satisfy integral Cartan pairings with all roots. They form a lattice Λ containing the root lattice Λ_r with finite index, with basis of fundamental dominant weights relative to Δ; the source records Λ/Λ_r for every irreducible type.
search_key: abstract weight lattice and fundamental group table
mapping_hint: integral-weight and simple-root coordinate data are native; abstract weight-lattice quotient/table remains absent

label: dominant weights and root order
source_data: A weight is dominant when its fundamental-weight coordinates are nonnegative. Each W-orbit contains a unique dominant weight; λ≥μ when λ−μ is a nonnegative integral sum of positive roots, and dominant λ satisfies λ≥wλ for all w∈W.
mapping_hint: dominance and root order are direct coordinate predicates; unique dominant orbit representative and λ≥wλ theorem remain absent

label: dual root system
source_data: The coroots α∨=2α/(α,α) form the dual root system Φ∨. Its Cartan matrix is transposed, its Weyl group is canonically W, and simple coroots are the dual linear functions characterized by value 2 on their root and 0 on the other fundamental weights.
mapping_hint: dual root system itself is library-owned; canonical Weyl-group/Cartan comparison is only partial
